# Cancer Detection System

## System Overview

The cancer detection system integrates multiple imaging modalities and computational modeling techniques to reconstruct biophysical properties of tissue, thereby enabling more accurate identification of cancerous regions. The system is architected around several interconnected components that work in concert to produce, refine, and validate biophysical models of the imaged anatomy.

## Imaging Systems

At its foundation, the cancer detection system comprises at least two imaging systems, with each system implementing a different imaging modality. By employing distinct modalities—such as, for example, magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, or positron emission tomography—the system captures complementary information about the same underlying tissue. Each imaging system acquires and provides sampled image data, which serves as the empirical reference against which computational models are evaluated.

## Modeling Units

For each imaging modality, a dedicated modeling unit produces modeled image data. Critically, each modeling unit generates its output based on a common set of biophysical parameters. This shared parameter set ensures that all modeled representations derive from a unified physical description of the tissue, notwithstanding the differences between the imaging modalities. In this way, the modeling units translate a single underlying biophysical model into the respective domains of each imaging technique.

## Joint Non-Linear Inversion Module

A joint non-linear inversion module receives information from each of the modeling units. By simultaneously incorporating data derived from all modalities, this module reconstructs a set of joint biophysical properties. The non-linear inversion approach allows the system to solve the complex, coupled relationships between the observed image data and the underlying tissue characteristics, yielding a consolidated set of properties that is consistent across all imaging modalities.

## Scaling Unit

Following reconstruction, a scaling unit revises the common set of biophysical parameters based on the reconstructed set of joint biophysical properties. This feedback mechanism refines the parameters that drive the modeling units, allowing the system to iteratively improve the fidelity of its models. Through successive revisions, the common parameter set converges toward values that more accurately represent the true biophysical state of the imaged tissue.

## Comparator

Finally, a comparator evaluates the accuracy of the modeling process. For each imaging system, the comparator compares the sampled image data against the corresponding modeled image data. It then determines whether the difference between the two falls below a predetermined threshold. When this condition is satisfied, the modeled data is considered a sufficiently faithful representation of the observed data, indicating that the reconstructed biophysical properties are reliable. If the difference exceeds the threshold, further iterations of modeling, inversion, and parameter scaling may be performed until convergence is achieved.

## Conclusion

Together, these components form an iterative, multi-modal framework in which biophysical parameters are continually modeled, jointly inverted, and refined until the resulting models align closely with the acquired image data. This integrated approach enhances the precision of cancer detection by grounding the analysis in a physically consistent, cross-modality reconstruction of tissue properties.

# Multi-Modal Cancer Detection System Using a Unified Biophysical Framework

## Overview

The present system provides an advanced approach to cancer detection by integrating multiple imaging modalities within a single, unified computational framework. Rather than analyzing images from different sources in isolation, the system combines complementary data streams to reconstruct a shared set of underlying biophysical properties, thereby improving both the accuracy and reliability of cancer detection.

## Integration of Multiple Imaging Modalities

At the core of the system is the integration of at least two distinct imaging modalities. Each modality—which may include, for example, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), ultrasound, or other diagnostic techniques—captures a different aspect of the underlying tissue. Each modality independently provides sampled image data, representing the physical measurements obtained from the region of interest.

Because different imaging techniques are sensitive to different tissue characteristics, no single modality typically captures the complete picture of a suspected lesion. By combining several modalities, the system leverages their complementary strengths, allowing features that may be ambiguous or invisible in one modality to be resolved through information provided by another.

## Modeling Units and Common Biophysical Parameters

To unify these disparate data sources, the system employs a set of modeling units. Critically, these modeling units are built upon a **common set of biophysical parameters**—physical quantities that describe the actual state and composition of the tissue, such as cell density, vascularity, diffusion characteristics, metabolic activity, or tissue mechanical properties.

Each modeling unit is responsible for predicting how a given imaging modality would respond to a particular set of biophysical parameters. In other words, the modeling units act as forward models: they translate the shared underlying biophysical description of the tissue into predicted (modeled) image data specific to each modality. Because all modeling units draw from the same common parameter set, they are inherently linked, ensuring physical consistency across modalities.

## Joint Non-Linear Inversion

The relationship between the biophysical parameters and the resulting image data is generally complex and non-linear. To recover the true biophysical properties from the observed measurements, the system incorporates a **joint non-linear inversion module**.

This module performs an inversion process—working backward from the sampled image data to estimate the biophysical parameters that produced it. Because the inversion is performed *jointly* across all imaging modalities simultaneously, the reconstructed biophysical properties must be consistent with every available data source at once. This joint approach substantially constrains the solution, reducing ambiguity and improving robustness compared to inverting each modality separately.

## Iterative Refinement via the Scaling Unit

The reconstruction proceeds iteratively. Beginning with an initial estimate of the biophysical parameters, the modeling units generate corresponding modeled image data, which is then compared against the actual sampled data. Based on this comparison, the parameters are progressively refined.

A **scaling unit** governs this refinement process, adjusting the parameters between iterations to bring the modeled data into closer agreement with the sampled data. Through successive iterations, the estimated biophysical properties converge toward values that best explain all of the observed measurements simultaneously.

## Comparator and Threshold-Based Detection

To determine when the reconstruction is sufficiently accurate—and to ultimately support the detection decision—the system includes a **comparator**. This component evaluates the difference between the sampled image data and the modeled image data.

The comparator measures this difference against a predefined **threshold**. When the discrepancy falls below the threshold, the modeled reconstruction is deemed to faithfully represent the underlying tissue, and the recovered biophysical parameters can be relied upon for diagnostic interpretation. Deviations, patterns, or parameter values indicative of malignancy can then be identified with high confidence.

## Advantages of the Unified Approach

By combining multiple imaging modalities within a single biophysical framework, rather than treating each independently, the system achieves several key benefits:

- **Improved accuracy:** Joint inversion constrains the reconstruction using all available data, reducing errors and false detections.
- **Physical consistency:** A shared parameter set ensures that the reconstructed tissue properties are physically meaningful across all modalities.
- **Robustness:** Complementary modalities compensate for the limitations and uncertainties inherent in any single imaging technique.
- **Iterative precision:** The scaling unit and comparator work together to progressively refine and validate the reconstruction until a reliable result is achieved.

## Conclusion

In summary, this cancer detection system unifies at least two imaging modalities through modeling units grounded in a common set of biophysical parameters. A joint non-linear inversion module reconstructs the shared biophysical properties, which are iteratively refined by a scaling unit and validated by a comparator against a threshold. This integrated, multi-modal, biophysically-grounded approach enables more accurate and reliable cancer detection than conventional single-modality methods.

## "The": The Little Word That Runs the Language

Of all the words in the English language, none works harder than "the." It is the most frequently used word in English, appearing in roughly one out of every sixteen words we read or speak. Small, unassuming, and easy to overlook, "the" is the quiet engine that keeps our sentences running smoothly.

**What it does**

"The" is the definite article. Its job is to point—to signal that a noun refers to something specific and identifiable rather than something general. Compare "I saw a dog" with "I saw the dog." The first introduces an unknown creature; the second assumes you already know which dog we mean. In that single letter's worth of difference lies a whole world of shared understanding between speaker and listener.

**A surprising history**

"The" descends from Old English, where the language once used a more complex system of articles that changed form depending on gender, number, and grammatical case. Over centuries, English shed most of this complexity, and the many variations collapsed into the single, dependable word we use today. Its spelling stabilized, but its pronunciation still shifts subtly: we say "thuh" before consonants and "thee" before vowels.

**Why it matters**

For learners of English, "the" is famously tricky, because many languages have no articles at all. Knowing when to include it—and when to leave it out—can take years to master. Yet for native speakers, it operates almost invisibly, a reflex rather than a decision.

In the end, "the" is proof that importance has nothing to do with size. It carries no dramatic meaning of its own, yet it shapes clarity, specificity, and flow in nearly every sentence we build.

## Multi-Modal Cancer Detection System Using Joint Non-Linear Inversion for Biophysical Property Reconstruction

**Abstract**

A system and method for detecting cancerous tissue by reconstructing biophysical tissue properties from complementary imaging modalities using a joint non-linear inversion framework. The system comprises a first imaging modality configured to acquire a first dataset representative of a first physical signal propagating through a target tissue region, and a second imaging modality configured to acquire a second dataset representative of a second, physically distinct signal propagating through the same target tissue region. A joint inversion processor is configured to reconstruct a set of shared biophysical parameters—including at least one of tissue stiffness, acoustic impedance, dielectric permittivity, perfusion, or mass density—by simultaneously minimizing a coupled objective function that relates both datasets to a unified physical forward model. The joint non-linear inversion enforces structural cross-gradient or physics-based coupling constraints between the modalities, thereby resolving ambiguities inherent to single-modality reconstruction and improving spatial resolution and quantitative accuracy of the recovered parameter maps. A classification module analyzes the jointly reconstructed biophysical parameter maps to identify one or more regions exhibiting biophysical signatures characteristic of malignancy, and generates an output indicative of a probability, location, or extent of cancerous tissue within the target region. In certain embodiments, the two imaging modalities comprise ultrasound tomography and microwave tomography, or elastography and diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, wherein the coupled forward model accounts for the distinct wave-physics or transport governing each modality.

---

**Illustrative Independent Claim:**

**1.** A multi-modal cancer detection system comprising:

a first imaging subsystem configured to generate a first measurement dataset from a target tissue region based on a first physical propagation mechanism;

a second imaging subsystem configured to generate a second measurement dataset from said target tissue region based on a second physical propagation mechanism distinct from the first;

a joint inversion processor configured to:
   (a) define a coupled forward model relating a shared set of biophysical parameters to both the first and second measurement datasets;

a classification module configured to identify, from the reconstructed biophysical parameters, at least one region satisfying a predetermined malignancy criterion and to output an indication of detected cancerous tissue.

# Multimodal Convergent Imaging System (MCIS)

## Overview

A medical imaging system that jointly reconstructs images from two complementary modalities by treating them as different observations of the *same underlying tissue*, described through a **shared set of biophysical parameters**. Rather than reconstructing each modality separately and fusing afterward, the system iteratively refines a unified tissue model until the *predicted* signals for both modalities match the *acquired* data.

---

## Core Innovation

The invention's key insight is a **shared biophysical parameter map** `θ(x)` defined over the imaging volume, where each voxel `x` carries physically meaningful quantities such as:

- Tissue density / proton density
- Water/fat fraction
- Perfusion and vascular permeability
- Local relaxation properties or acoustic impedance
- Tracer/contrast concentration

These parameters simultaneously drive the physics of **both** imaging modalities.

---

## System Architecture

**1. Dual Acquisition Front-End**
Two co-registered modalities are acquired, for example:
- MRI + PET
- Ultrasound + Photoacoustic
- CT + MRI

**2. Forward Models (per modality)**
Two differentiable physics simulators:
- `F_A(θ) → predicted data for modality A`
- `F_B(θ) → predicted data for modality B`

Each encodes the governing equations of its modality (signal equations, attenuation, wave propagation, etc.).

**3. Shared Parameter Engine**
A single latent representation `θ` feeds both forward models—enforcing that both modalities remain physically consistent with one common tissue description.

**4. Iterative Refinement Loop**

```
Initialize θ₀
Repeat:
    predicted_A = F_A(θ)
    predicted_B = F_B(θ)
    loss = ||predicted_A − measured_A||²
         + ||predicted_B − measured_B||²
         + R(θ)              # regularization / priors
    θ ← θ − η · ∇θ(loss)     # gradient-based update
Until convergence (both residuals below threshold)
```

**5. Convergence Criterion**
Iteration halts when *modeled* and *sampled* data agree across **both** modalities within tolerance, and parameter updates stabilize.

---

## Novel Elements (Claim-Worthy)

| Element | Distinction from Prior Art |
|---|---|
| Shared biophysical parameters | Modalities constrain each other, not fused post-hoc |
| Joint differentiable forward models | Enables end-to-end gradient optimization |
| Cross-modal convergence stopping rule | Consistency across modalities defines completion |
| Physics-informed priors | Reduces artifacts and dose/scan time |

---

## Advantages

- **Reduced acquisition burden** — sparse data from one modality is compensated by the other via the shared model.
- **Physically consistent output** — one tissue model, not two conflicting images.
- **Quantitative maps** — outputs interpretable biophysical parameters, not just intensities.
- **Artifact suppression** — cross-modal constraints reject inconsistent noise.

---

## Example Embodiment

A PET–MRI scanner where PET tracer kinetics and MRI relaxation both depend on shared perfusion and tissue-composition parameters. Low-count PET data (reduced radiotracer dose) is stabilized by MRI anatomical constraints, while PET metabolic information sharpens MRI parameter estimation—both refined until convergence.

---

# Technical Summary: Multi-Modal Cancer Detection Apparatus

## Overview

The disclosed apparatus provides an integrated system for detecting cancerous tissue through the coordinated operation of multiple imaging modalities, computational modeling, and comparative analysis. By fusing complementary datasets and reconciling them through joint inversion, the apparatus achieves improved detection sensitivity and specificity relative to single-modality systems.

---

## System Components

### 1. Multiple Imaging Systems

The apparatus incorporates two or more imaging systems configured to acquire spatially registered data from a target region of tissue. Representative modalities include:

- **Optical/diffuse optical imaging** for measuring tissue absorption and scattering properties
- **Ultrasound or elastography** for characterizing mechanical and acoustic properties
- **Electrical impedance/microwave imaging** for mapping dielectric contrast
- **Magnetic resonance or X-ray-based imaging** for structural reference

Each imaging system generates a distinct measurement dataset representing a physical property distribution across a shared coordinate space.

### 2. Modeling Units

A dedicated **modeling unit** is associated with each imaging system. Each modeling unit generates a forward model that predicts the expected measurement response given an assumed distribution of tissue properties. The modeling units:

- Discretize the target region into a common voxel or mesh grid
- Apply modality-specific physics (e.g., wave propagation, diffusion, or conduction equations)
- Output modeled response data for comparison against acquired measurements

### 3. Joint Inversion Module

The **joint inversion module** receives the outputs of the multiple modeling units and reconstructs a unified set of tissue property distributions. The module:

- Solves a coupled inverse problem across all modalities simultaneously
- Applies **structural coupling constraints** (e.g., cross-gradient or shared-boundary regularization) to enforce consistency among the reconstructed property maps
- Iteratively minimizes a joint objective function combining data misfit terms from each modality with regularization terms
- Outputs co-registered property maps that share common structural features, reducing artifacts inherent in independent reconstructions

### 4. Scaling Unit

Because each modality reports property values in different physical units and dynamic ranges, a **scaling unit** normalizes the reconstructed outputs. The scaling unit:

- Applies modality-specific scaling factors, weights, or normalization transforms
- Converts heterogeneous property values into a common, comparable metric space
- Optionally applies calibration data derived from reference or phantom measurements
- Produces scaled parameter values suitable for direct combination or comparison

### 5. Comparator

The **comparator** evaluates the scaled tissue property values to identify regions indicative of malignancy. The comparator:

- Compares scaled values against one or more predetermined thresholds or reference profiles characteristic of healthy versus cancerous tissue
- Combines multi-modal indicators (e.g., via weighted scoring or classification logic)
- Flags voxels or regions exceeding the malignancy criteria
- Generates an output indication, such as a probability map or binary classification, identifying suspected cancerous tissue

---

## Operational Flow

1. The multiple imaging systems concurrently acquire spatially registered measurement data from the target tissue region.
2. Each modeling unit generates predicted responses based on assumed property distributions.
3. The joint inversion module reconstructs coupled property maps consistent across all modalities.
4. The scaling unit normalizes the reconstructed values into a common metric space.
5. The comparator evaluates the scaled values against reference criteria and outputs an indication of suspected cancerous tissue.

---

## Technical Advantages

- **Enhanced accuracy** through fusion of complementary physical contrasts
- **Reduced reconstruction artifacts** via structurally coupled joint inversion
- **Consistent comparison** enabled by normalized, scaled outputs
- **Improved diagnostic confidence** through multi-modal corroboration of detected regions

---

*Note: This summary is intended as a technical description of an apparatus and its subsystems. It is not a substitute for regulatory clearance documentation or clinical validation, which would be required before diagnostic deployment.*

counterfactuals.output:
# Multimodal Data Fusion for Cancer Detection via Biophysical Modeling

## Core Concept

The approach you're describing is a form of **model-based image fusion** where instead of simply overlaying or statistically combining two images, the system uses a shared physical model to interpret both modalities simultaneously. The key insight is that different imaging modalities respond to the *same underlying tissue properties* through different physical mechanisms.

## The Common Biophysical Parameter Layer

The foundation is identifying tissue parameters that influence both modalities. Cancer alters tissue in characteristic ways:

- **Cellularity / cell density** – tumors often have densely packed cells
- **Vascularity / blood volume** – angiogenesis increases perfusion
- **Vessel permeability** – leaky tumor vasculature
- **Oxygenation / hypoxia** – metabolic changes
- **Water content / diffusion** – altered extracellular space
- **Stiffness / elastic modulus** – tumors are often mechanically stiffer

These parameters form a **shared state space** that both imaging modalities can be predicted from.

## The Forward Model Framework

For each modality, you construct a **forward model** — a mathematical mapping from biophysical parameters to expected signal:

```
Modality A signal = f_A(biophysical parameters)
Modality B signal = f_B(biophysical parameters)
```

**Example pairing — DCE-MRI + Diffuse Optical Tomography:**
- MRI contrast enhancement depends on blood volume and permeability (via pharmacokinetic models like Tofts model)
- Optical absorption depends on hemoglobin concentration (also tied to blood volume/oxygenation)

Both modalities are functions of overlapping vascular parameters.

## The Inverse Problem (Fusion Step)

Rather than analyzing each image independently, you **jointly estimate** the biophysical parameters that best explain *both* measured images at once:

```
Find parameters θ that minimize:

   ||I_A_measured − f_A(θ)||²  +  ||I_B_measured − f_B(θ)||²  +  R(θ)
```

Where:
- The first two terms measure agreement between predicted and measured images
- **R(θ)** is a regularization/prior term (spatial smoothness, anatomical constraints)

This is solved iteratively (e.g., gradient descent, Bayesian inference):

1. Guess initial parameter maps
2. Run forward models to predict both images
3. Compare predictions to measurements
4. Update parameters to reduce error
5. Repeat until convergence

## Why This Beats Simple Fusion

| Simple Fusion | Model-Based Fusion |
|---|---|
| Overlays images post-hoc | Integrates at physical level |
| Weaknesses of each modality persist | Modalities *constrain* each other |
| No interpretable output | Yields biophysical maps |
| Sensitive to registration errors | Physics provides coupling |

The critical advantage: **cross-modality constraints**. A low-resolution but quantitative modality can regularize a high-resolution but ambiguous one. Noise or artifacts inconsistent across modalities get suppressed because they can't be explained by a single physical state.

## Cancer Detection Decision

Once you have estimated biophysical parameter maps:

1. **Classify voxels/regions** using thresholds or machine learning on the physical parameters (e.g., high vascularity + high cellularity + high stiffness → suspicious)
2. **Compute residuals** — regions where the model *fails* to fit both images may indicate abnormal tissue
3. **Quantify confidence** via posterior uncertainty (in a Bayesian formulation)

## Practical Considerations

- **Registration**: Images must be spatially aligned so voxels correspond to the same tissue
- **Model validity**: Forward models must be accurate; oversimplification biases results
- **Computational cost**: Joint inversion is expensive
- **Identifiability**: Ensure the two modalities actually provide complementary (not redundant) information about the parameters
- **Validation**: Biopsy/histopathology as ground truth

---

# Dual-Modality Tumor Imaging System with Joint Non-Linear Inversion and Threshold-Based Comparison

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to medical imaging systems, and more particularly to a dual-modality imaging apparatus configured to perform joint non-linear inversion of acquired signal data and threshold-based comparison for the detection, localization, and characterization of tumor tissue.

## BACKGROUND

Conventional single-modality imaging systems often provide incomplete or ambiguous representations of suspected tumor regions, particularly where anatomical contrast is low or where functional and structural information must be correlated. There remains a need for an integrated system capable of combining complementary imaging modalities and reconstructing tissue property distributions through a unified computational framework.

## SUMMARY

In accordance with one embodiment, a system is provided comprising a first imaging subsystem and a second imaging subsystem of differing modality, a data acquisition module, a joint non-linear inversion processor, and a threshold-based comparison module operatively coupled to generate a diagnostic output indicative of tumor presence.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE COMPONENTS

### First Imaging Subsystem (110)

The first imaging subsystem **110** comprises a first energy source configured to direct interrogating energy of a first modality toward a target volume of biological tissue. In one embodiment, said first modality comprises electromagnetic radiation in a defined frequency band. The subsystem further includes a first array of detectors positioned to receive scattered, transmitted, or emitted energy returning from the target volume and to generate a first set of measurement signals.

### Second Imaging Subsystem (120)

The second imaging subsystem **120** comprises a second energy source configured to direct interrogating energy of a second modality, distinct from said first modality, toward substantially the same target volume. In one embodiment, said second modality comprises acoustic or ultrasonic energy. A second array of detectors is arranged to receive returning energy and to generate a second set of measurement signals.

### Registration and Acquisition Module (130)

A data acquisition module **130** is operatively coupled to the first and second detector arrays and configured to sample, digitize, and temporally correlate the first and second sets of measurement signals. A spatial registration unit establishes a common coordinate frame such that measurements from both modalities are mapped to corresponding spatial locations within the target volume.

### Joint Non-Linear Inversion Processor (140)

A processing subsystem **140** is configured to execute a joint non-linear inversion procedure. In operation, the processor:

**(a)** initializes an estimated distribution of one or more tissue parameters over a discretized reconstruction domain representing the target volume;

**(b)** computes, by means of a forward model, predicted measurement signals for each modality corresponding to the current estimated parameter distribution, wherein said forward model characterizes the non-linear relationship between the tissue parameters and the measured energy;

**(c)** determines a residual between the predicted measurement signals and the acquired measurement signals for each modality;

**(d)** forms a joint objective function combining the residuals of the first and second modalities, optionally weighted by respective confidence factors and augmented by one or more regularization terms enforcing spatial or cross-modality coupling constraints;

**(e)** iteratively updates the estimated parameter distribution to reduce said joint objective function, employing a non-linear optimization scheme such as a gradient-based, Gauss-Newton, or Levenberg-Marquardt update; and

**(f)** outputs, upon satisfaction of a convergence criterion, a reconstructed multi-parameter map of the target volume.

The joint formulation permits information derived from the first modality to constrain and stabilize the reconstruction of the second modality, and vice versa, thereby mitigating ill-posedness inherent to either modality considered independently.

### Threshold-Based Comparison Module (150)

A comparison module **150** receives the reconstructed multi-parameter map and applies at least one threshold criterion to identify candidate regions. In one embodiment, the module:

**(a)** compares one or more reconstructed parameter values at each spatial location against a predetermined or adaptively determined threshold value;

**(b)** designates locations satisfying said threshold as candidate tumor voxels;

**(c)** optionally applies a combined criterion wherein a location is designated as tumor-indicative only when parameters derived from both modalities jointly satisfy respective thresholds; and

**(d)** aggregates contiguous candidate voxels into segmented regions and computes associated metrics such as volume, centroid, and boundary extent.

### Output and Display Subsystem (160)

An output subsystem **160** generates a visual, numerical, or coded representation of the identified regions, superimposed upon or fused with an anatomical reference image, and presents the diagnostic output to an operator.

## OPERATION

In a representative mode of operation, the target volume is sequentially or simultaneously interrogated by the first and second imaging subsystems. The acquisition module **130** registers and digitizes the resulting signals. The joint non-linear inversion processor **140** reconstructs a spatially resolved multi-parameter map by iteratively minimizing the combined objective function. The threshold-based comparison module **150** evaluates the reconstructed map against one or more criteria to delineate tumor-indicative regions, and the output subsystem **160** presents the resulting characterization.

## CLAIMS (EXEMPLARY)

**1.** A dual-modality tumor imaging system comprising: a first imaging subsystem of a first modality; a second imaging subsystem of a second modality distinct from the first; a data acquisition module configured to spatially register measurement signals from both subsystems; a processor configured to perform a joint non-linear inversion of the registered signals to produce a reconstructed multi-parameter map; and a comparison module configured to apply at least one threshold criterion to said map to identify a tumor-indicative region.

**2.** The system of claim 1, wherein the joint non-linear inversion minimizes an objective function combining residuals of both modalities subject to a regularization constraint.

**3.** The system of claim 1, wherein the comparison module designates a location as tumor-indicative only when reconstructed parameters from both modalities jointly satisfy respective thresholds.

**4.** The system of claim 1, wherein the first modality comprises electromagnetic energy and the second modality comprises acoustic energy.

**5.** The system of claim 2, wherein the regularization constraint enforces cross-modality structural coupling between the reconstructed parameters.
